fdroid:com.rrajath.grove.name: Bloom: Org-mode Notes & Tasks
fdroid:com.rrajath.grove.summary: A native Org-mode notes app for Android. Your notes stay plain .org files.
fdroid:com.rrajath.grove.description:
Bloom is a native Android Org-mode note-taking app, built as a first-class mobile companion for Emacs org-mode users.
Bloom edits plain .org files in a folder you choose. There is no account, no proprietary database, and no export step: the files on disk are your notes, byte-for-byte, and they sync to your other machines with whatever tool you already trust (Syncthing is the recommended pairing). If you stop using Bloom tomorrow, your notes are exactly where they always were.
Features:
* File-first: .org files in a synced folder are the sole source of truth. Bloom's internal database is only a rebuildable search index.
* Lossless org engine: a custom parser models documents as a thin view over the raw text, so parsing and writing a file back out is byte-identical by construction. Bloom never reformats a file it didn't deliberately edit.
* Zero-friction capture: org-capture style templates with placeholders for the current time, a prompt, and cursor position. Targets include the top or bottom of a file, under a heading (by name or CUSTOM_ID), and year/month/day datetrees. Reachable from a home-screen widget, the share sheet, an optional persistent notification, and deep links.
* Home-screen widgets: a one-tap Capture widget, and an Agenda ledger widget showing overdue and upcoming tasks with mark-done and quick-add, without opening the app.
* Real editor: raw org subtree editing with syntax highlighting, a formatting toolbar, list continuation on Enter, a metadata sheet for TODO state, priority, and tags, SCHEDULED/DEADLINE editing, repeater advancement on DONE, and autosave with a stale-file guard.
* Scheduling: a full-screen editor puts SCHEDULED and DEADLINE on the same calendar, with presets, a time range, an org repeater, and a shorthand box that parses lines like "fri 10-11am ++1w" as you type.
* Reminders: a notification fires when a heading's SCHEDULED or DEADLINE time arrives, with Complete and Reschedule actions on the notification itself.
* Outline operations: a collapsible heading tree with body previews, expand/collapse all, move/cut/copy/paste subtrees, cycle TODO state by swipe, and narrow to a subtree.
* Search: Orgzly-compatible search syntax, saved searches, and an agenda view, backed by a SQLite FTS5 index so substring search stays fast as the vault grows.
* Sync that respects your tools: change detection by file revision, Syncthing conflict-file detection with a keep-local, keep-remote, or keep-both picker, manual and continuous sync modes, and .orgzlyignore support.
* A calm, deliberate design: IBM Plex Sans/Serif/Mono, 20 light and dark themes led by Bloom Light and Bloom Dark, and org syntax highlighting colored the way an Emacs theme would.
Bloom has no server-side component. Its only network request is fetching a page title when you share a link into Bloom, to use as the note heading. Sites that hide the title behind a script are loaded in a hidden WebView with JavaScript enabled. Turn this off in Settings, Sharing, Fetch link titles, and Bloom makes no network request at all; a shared link is then labeled with the title the sharing app provided, if any, or the URL.
Bloom was formerly known as Grove.

fdroid:io.github.munzzyy.tern.name: Tern
fdroid:io.github.munzzyy.tern.summary: Follow app releases where they are published and check them before they install
fdroid:io.github.munzzyy.tern.description:
A lot of good Android apps never reach a store, or reach it days late. Their developers put releases on GitHub, GitLab, Codeberg, a repository they run, or a plain web page. Tern follows those places for you. Paste a link or share one from the browser and it figures out what it is looking at.
Then it checks the file, because a release page can be tampered with and a download can be swapped on the way.
The signature has to be from the same certificate as the app already on your phone. Tern remembers that certificate from the first install, and your export carries it to your next phone.
If the publisher gave a checksum, the file has to match it.
The file has to be the app you asked for, and not an older version of it.
Tern reads the version and the signer out of a file while it is still on the server, a few kilobytes of it, so an update is only offered when there really is one.
On Android 12 and newer, updates go in without asking once Tern has installed the app. With Shizuku or Dhizuku they go in without asking, first installs too. If Android does want a confirmation, you get a notification you can update from. Background checks use Android's own scheduler, as often as every 15 minutes, and you choose whether they run on mobile data or only while charging.
No account. Nothing is reported to anyone. HTTPS only.
Works on phones, tablets and Android TV, where the remote is all you need. On a TV, choose Send from a phone: scan the code it shows, and your phone sends links or your app list, sealed with that code so nobody else on the network can read or change them.
Choose Orbot in the settings and everything Tern sends goes through Tor. If Orbot is not there, nothing is sent at all.
For well-known apps Tern already carries the developer's certificate, so even the first install is checked. Make it look the way you like: colors from your wallpaper or your own, contrast, density, corners and icon shapes.
English and 28 other languages; the translations are machine-made and corrections are welcome.
Obtainium user? Import your export file and your apps come along, with every option they had. Tern writes Obtainium's format too.
Sort, group and filter your list, give categories colors, and see what is waiting on a home-screen widget or a Quick Settings tile.
Reads: GitHub releases and Actions builds, GitLab, Forgejo, Gitea, Codeberg, F-Droid, IzzyOnDroid, any F-Droid format repository (signature checked), web pages, direct links, Jenkins, SourceHut, SourceForge, itch.io, Telegram and Neutron Code.
Off until you turn them on in Settings: the third-party stores APKPure, Aptoide, APKCombo, APKMirror (tracking only), Tencent, Huawei AppGallery, Samsung Galaxy Store and vivo. A store serves its own copies of apps, not files from the developer's own site, and Tern says so. The first install from a store decides which certificate later updates must carry, unless Tern already knows the developer's. Tern does not read sites that offer modified apps, or stores that answer only their own app.
Who Tern talks to: the forges, repositories, instances and sites of the apps you add; for an F-Droid app also F-Droid's data on gitlab.com and the changelog it names; the icon hosts of those sources, such as raw.githubusercontent.com; a third-party store's own hosts only when stores are on and you add an app from it; and the places you tick when you search, which are GitHub, Codeberg, GitLab and search.f-droid.org at first. Every request says it comes from Tern. PRIVACY.md lists every host.

These printers are often erroneously referred to as winprinters or GDI printers. However, Microsoft GDI only mandates the API between an application and the printer driver, not the protocol on the wire between the printer driver and the printer. In fact, HBPL printers are raster printers which happen to use a very efficient wire protocol. HBPL is just one of many wire protocols that are in use today, such as Postscript, PCL, Epson, ZjStream, etc.

firefox-addons:3105444.name: DNSAudit.io - DNS Security & Attack Surface
firefox-addons:3105444.summary: Check the DNS security and attack surface of any domain in one click. DNSAudit reads the public DNS of the site you are on and shows a quick, factual snapshot across five tabs, then links you to the full DNS security report when you want the graded f
firefox-addons:3105444.description:
Check the DNS security and attack surface of any domain in one click. DNSAudit reads the public DNS of the site you are on and shows a quick, factual snapshot across five tabs, then links you to the full DNS security report when you want the graded findings and fixes.
DNS is part of your security posture. Misconfigured email authentication, missing DNSSEC, permissive CAA, or forgotten hostnames that still resolve all widen a domain's attack surface. This extension surfaces those signals fast, straight from the tab you are on.
Overview: a DNS security posture read by area, an exposure summary, and the last DNSAudit grade when the domain has been scanned before.
Email authentication: SPF with its qualifier and DNS lookup count, DKIM at common selectors, DMARC policy and reporting, MTA-STS and TLS-RPT.
DNS integrity: DNSSEC, the certificate authorities allowed by CAA, DANE/TLSA, a wildcard check, and a DNS rebinding check that flags private IPs in public records.
Infrastructure: nameservers and their provider, IPv4 and IPv6, and mail servers.
Attack surface exposure: integrations detected from TXT records, reverse DNS with the forward-confirmed (FCrDNS) check, and common sensitive hostnames that resolve, such as admin, vpn, staging or api.
Hover any row to see the record behind it. It is a fast factual look, not a verdict. The graded findings, severities, and recommended fixes live in the full report on DNSAudit.io .
The snapshot is read live from public DNS over HTTPS, the same data anyone can query. The extension only looks up the domain you choose. It does not read page content and does not track the sites you visit. The quick look needs no account.

firefox-addons:2937387.description: This add-on is a starter AI Ad Block extension. • The uploaded .zip is the Firefox-compatible build (no rules/ directory, uses background.scripts instead of service_worker). • The uploaded source .zip contains the full, human-readable source code (TypeScript, scripts, manifests, build files) without dist/ or node_modules/. • No remote code execution, dynamic code generation, or obfuscated code is used. • Can detect hidden ads, sponsored labels, promoted posts, native ads that rule-based systems miss. • Can adapt better if you re-train the model with new data. * Sync your book library between multiple devices
* View and share your book collection online

apple-macos:6760869971.name: Undercast Weather Aether
apple-macos:6760869971.description:
UndercastWeather Aether delivers forecasts alongside on-device, model-enhanced predictions you can compare side by side. In the United States those forecasts come from the National Weather Service and are refined by Aether. Everywhere else they come from Apple Weather, refined by Aether overtime.
The idea is simple: you should be able to see the official forecast AND a smarter interpretation of it — without giving up your privacy.
WHAT MAKES UNDERCAST DIFFERENT
• Dual-mode forecasts — switch between raw NWS data and Aether-enhanced predictions with a tap
• On-device learning — Aether refines its forecasts using local signals; nothing leaves your device
• Worldwide coverage — forecasts, alerts and UV for places outside the US from Apple Weather, shown as provided
• Severe weather Live Activities — Tornado, Thunderstorm, Flood, and other warnings appear on your Lock Screen and in the Dynamic Island, with hazard-specific icons
• Astronomical data — sunrise, sunset, moon phase, and twilight times sourced from the U.S. Naval Observatory
• Backup sources — if a weather service can't be reached, the app switches to another and tells you which one it used
• Weather map — temperature, radar, wind, precipitation and air quality for the lower 48 states, and a worldwide rain layer from NASA elsewhere
• Searchable — find a place by city or ZIP code, no location sharing required
BUILT FOR APPLE PLATFORMS
Native experiences on Mac, iPhone, and iPad — with a Home Screen widget for at-a-glance conditions.
ONGOING UPDATES
UndercastWeather regularly updates Aether to improve accuracy, performance, and features.
PRIVACY FIRST
Aether's learning happens on device. Your trained data never leaves your devices — with optional iCloud sync, it moves only between your Apple devices through your private iCloud account. You don't need to share your location to use the app, and we don't collect telemetry on your forecast usage.
Our apps do not use third-party analytics, advertising SDKs, tracking SDKs, or data brokers. We encourage every user to turn on Apple's App Privacy Report to see this for themselves.
To enable App Privacy Report on iPhone or iPad, open Settings > Privacy & Security > App Privacy Report > Turn On App Privacy Report. After you use the app for a while, iOS will show the network domains contacted by the app.
For our weather app, expected network activity is limited to Apple-operated services (App Store, iCloud, Apple Weather and system functions) and direct connections to the public sources of the data you asked for: NOAA and the National Weather Service, the EPA and AirNow, the U.S. Naval Observatory, NASA, and the public hosts those agencies publish through.
We believe privacy claims should be inspectable, not merely promised.
NOTE
Air quality is available in the United States only.
